newsitem.title: UK: Funds favour for oil keeps Brent over $20.
newsitem.headline: Funds favour for oil keeps Brent over $20.

text.p: Buoyant oil markets on Monday maintained their grip on $20 a barrel crude after last week's strong gains helped by renewed purchases by institutional funds.
London futures for benchmark North Sea Brent blend traded down 13 cents a barrel at $20.22 after jumping 85 cents on Friday.
"The funds have definitely stepped back in to oil but fundamentals have also played their part," said a London-based trader.
Dealers on Monday were reassessing market fundamentals in the light of Friday's price hike.
They said the the market's rise in part reflected increased demand for crude by European and U.S. refiners after the end of seasonal spring maintenance.
But traders warned that with refinery profit margins hit hard last week by crude's recent rise, refinery purchases might be stunted.
They said European refinery margins turned negative last week prompting some to reduce operations.
Markets have also found some support from further delays in new North Sea oilfield projects.

"Delays in the start-up of a number of non OPEC offshore oilfields are beginning to have an effect on output levels," said London's Centre for Global Energy Studies (CGES) in a report released on Monday.
Summer maintenance at North Sea oilfields is expected to trim some 260,000 barrels a day (bpd) from liftings in June at 4.35 million bpd compared to 4.61 million for May.
Analysts said oil markets now were looking finely balanced but that the chances of a supply led price slump had receded.

"When stockcover is low and information so hazy about the true level of oil demand and the exact level of production, it is difficult to be confident about where the oil price will head next," said the CGES. "What is clearer now is that a price meltdown is less likely."
Dealers are worried that higher oil prices may translate into a cancellation of some Iraqi crude liftings under the U.N.'s oil-for-food exchange.

Under the plan Iraq is permitted to sell $2 billion worth of crude over six months ending June 9. Last week's higher prices mean the financial target may be met more quickly than had been anticipated.
